title: Batch-confound audit for public transcriptomic datasets
description:
Reference implementation of a four-stage design-admissibility audit for public transcriptomic datasets, together with the derived results and figures for a methodological audit of 14 contrast-units across 12 GEO series in two disease domains (perioperative neurocognitive disorder and traumatic brain injury).

Public datasets are usually taken at face value: if the treatment arm is also the batch that ran on a different day, every downstream result is confounded and no downstream statistic reveals it. The audit applies four defences in order — (0) are the group labels independently verifiable; (1) is the batch real and is it entangled with the group, tested by a three-gate criterion combining structural entanglement, technical separability and nesting; (2) does the signal survive batch correction without moving globally; (3) is a module's identity asserted or tested against an external gene set — and returns one of four verdicts (stop / correct / proceed / normalize) per contrast-unit rather than per series.

Result: of the 14 contrast-units, 2 are unconditionally analysable, 6 only under documented restrictions, and 6 are categorically unusable. The original biological hypothesis (an m6A × programmed-cell-death signature) did not replicate across datasets (direction agreement 11/21 = 52.4%, p = 1.000). The audit is validated on a seeded simulation benchmark (99.4% correct verdicts, 497/500) and compared head-to-head against ComBat, sva and RUV, which in a collinear design retain 0.0%, 100% and 1.9% of the true signal respectively without warning.

All analyses use public GEO data (accessions tabulated in the repository); no new sequencing was performed. Raw GEO downloads are not shipped — only the small derived intermediates needed to regenerate every figure and number offline. The version-controlled source is at github.com/eagle-wk/pocd-batch-audit.
notes: Accompanies the manuscript "A diagnostic audit for batch and confounding artifacts in reuse of public bulk transcriptomic data: a two-domain study in perioperative neurocognitive disorder and traumatic brain injury" (under review; this record is the code and results archival release, not the article).
